summary: COSMIC COMPASS is an interactive astronomical exploration platform designed to make SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to everyone. The project aims to help users explore different regions of the sky using celestial coordinates, compare infrared observations across 102 wavelength bands, and investigate changes in astronomical sources over time. It also introduces scientific research into possible planets beyond our Solar System and moon-like companions. By combining astronomical visualization, scientific information, and interactive exploration, COSMIC COMPASS encourages students, researchers, and space enthusiasts to discover the universe.

COSMIC COMPASS

Exploring the Infrared Universe and the Search for Extragalactic Worlds

1. Introduction

The universe contains billions of galaxies, stars, planetary systems and mysterious celestial objects. Understanding these objects requires advanced astronomical observations and scientific data analysis.

COSMIC COMPASS is a proposed interactive astronomical exploration platform based on NASA's SPHEREx mission. It aims to make infrared astronomical observations easier to explore, compare and understand.

SPHEREx observes the entire sky in 102 infrared spectral bands, providing valuable information about galaxies, stars, interstellar dust and the evolution of the universe.

2. Problem Statement

Astronomical surveys generate enormous quantities of scientific data. However, accessing and interpreting these observations can be challenging for students, educators and members of the public.

There is a need for an accessible platform that allows users to explore astronomical locations, compare observations and understand the scientific information behind distant celestial objects.

3. Proposed Solution

COSMIC COMPASS proposes an interactive sky exploration system where users can enter celestial coordinates, including Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec), to investigate selected regions of the sky.

The platform is designed to connect astronomical images, observation dates, infrared wavelength information and source metadata in one accessible interface.

It also includes an educational research section exploring the scientific search for planets beyond the Milky Way.

4. Main Features

  1. Coordinate-based sky exploration using RA and Dec.
  2. Visualization of SPHEREx infrared observations.
  3. Exploration of 102 infrared spectral bands.
  4. Comparison of astronomical observations from different epochs.
  5. Image addition and subtraction for investigating possible changes.
  6. Identification and inspection of variable astronomical sources.
  7. Astronomical metadata and observation-quality information.
  8. Educational explanations of extragalactic planet research.
  9. Scientific references and data-source information.

5. Extragalactic Planets: Exploring Worlds Beyond the Milky Way

One of the most fascinating questions in modern astronomy is whether planets exist outside our own galaxy.

An important research candidate is M51-ULS-1b, associated with the Whirlpool Galaxy, also known as Messier 51, approximately 28 million light-years from Earth.

Researchers proposed this possible planet after observing a temporary decrease in X-ray emission from an X-ray binary system using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory.

The event lasted approximately three hours. A transiting planet is one possible explanation, but the candidate has not been confirmed.

COSMIC COMPASS will use this example to explain how astronomers search for distant planets and how scientific evidence is evaluated.

6. Extragalactic Moons and Moon-Like Companions

Moons beyond our Solar System are another exciting subject in astronomical research.

Astronomers investigate possible moon-like companions around planets and brown dwarfs using different observational techniques.

The project will explain the difference between an exomoon, a planet-mass companion and a possible extragalactic moon.

At present, no confirmed extragalactic exomoon is established by the scientific references used in this project.

7. Scientific Methods

The project introduces several important astronomical investigation methods:

  • Infrared astronomy: studying celestial objects through infrared radiation.
  • Multi-epoch observation: comparing images obtained at different times.
  • Spectral analysis: examining how astronomical sources appear across different wavelengths.
  • X-ray transit investigation: studying temporary reductions in X-ray brightness.
  • Gravitational microlensing: investigating distant planetary systems through gravitational magnification.

These methods help explain how astronomers investigate objects that are extremely far away.

8. Technology and Development

The proposed platform can use:

  • HTML and CSS for the interface.
  • JavaScript for interactive exploration.
  • Python for scientific data processing.
  • Astronomical image-processing techniques.
  • NASA SPHEREx public data and archive resources.
  • Interactive graphs and astronomical visualization.

The final implementation will distinguish working features from planned improvements.

9. Expected Impact

COSMIC COMPASS aims to:

  • Make astronomical observations easier to understand.
  • Encourage students to explore infrared astronomy.
  • Promote public awareness of NASA's SPHEREx mission.
  • Introduce the scientific search for extragalactic planets.
  • Encourage interest in planetary science and space exploration.
  • Connect astronomical discoveries with accessible scientific explanations.

10. Future Development

Future development may include improved astronomical image comparison, automated source detection, spectral visualization, additional space telescope datasets and advanced scientific analysis tools.

11. Conclusion

COSMIC COMPASS brings together infrared astronomy, interactive sky exploration and the search for distant planetary worlds.

By connecting astronomical observations with scientific explanations, the project aims to make the exploration of our universe more accessible, educational and inspiring.

Our goal is not only to explore the sky, but also to understand the discoveries and unanswered questions that make astronomy one of the most exciting fields of science.
